try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette: Mateo had spent decades moving with fluid certainty. Then came the rain-slicked curve on Route 9, the hydroplane, and the sickening lurch as the passenger door crumpled inward. Glass rained across his lap. When the other driver’s engine cut out, Mateo sat frozen, the smell of burnt rubber thick in his throat, convinced he would never walk again. He couldn’t explain it to his wife, Elena, that night. The image stayed locked behind his eyes, a tight, wordless knot that refused to unravel. In the weeks that followed, Mateo paced the studio floors, his eyes darting to emergency doors the moment he crossed the threshold. Every time he entered a rehearsal room, his gaze locked onto the nearest exit. This hypervigilance acted as a direct trigger for the event itself. Because he was so attuned to danger, the moment he heard a car door slam on the street below, the nonverbal memory of the crush would flood his system, and the sharp sounds of the airbag and bending metal would echo in his head. Each time those sounds and the accompanying shame rushed up, Mateo’s only recourse was to deliberately shut down. He forced his mind to leave his body until the images faded. To keep the silence at bay, he delayed sleep, staying up until three in the morning. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, telling himself that occupying his hands would keep the past buried. The habit only kept the memories jagged. By suppressing his thoughts and fragmenting his rest, Mateo denied his brain the chance to process the event. Instead of settling, the nonverbal memories grew heavier, and the auditory recalls became more frequent, returning uninvited whenever he allowed himself stillness. He began to interpret his exhaustion and emotional numbness as permanent damage. The deliberate blanking out and sleepless nights widened the gap between him and his former self. He came to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, convinced that the event had hollowed him out and left him incapable of the calm he once took for granted. That certainty only deepened the dread. Because he was convinced he couldn’t stop bad things from happening, his nervous system stayed permanently wired to scan for danger. His character blame—telling himself the accident happened because of the sort of person he was—fed a cycle of horror and guilt. When he felt those negative emotions spike, they reinforced his original fear, making him more likely to flinch at unexpected touches and track the exits. The constant alertness became its own prison. Elena would place a hand on his shoulder, and he would react with alarm so violently she would pull back. Over time, the perpetual threat monitoring convinced him that he was fundamentally unsafe and inherently flawed. Every flinch and exit count became proof that bad things were inevitable, and that his own nature was the reason he could never trust the world again. The cycle tightened over months. He stopped teaching advanced classes, citing a knee issue, but the real reason was the studio’s narrow backstage corridors and the way dancers still approached him with quick pats on the back. The avoidance cost him his livelihood and pulled Elena away. What finally brought Mateo to my office was a night he couldn’t suppress through. He walked past a car with flashing hazard lights, heard the rhythmic blinker, and experienced a full-body freeze. He sits on the edge of my couch now, afraid that if he stops holding himself together, he will shatter. He hopes, quietly, for a way to trust his own skin and step through a door without counting the exits.
